title: No Rush in Executing Atomic Instructions
problem: Modern x86 processors implement unfenced atomic RMW instructions (no implicit serializing fences), enabling eager execution as soon as operands are ready, but eager execution locks cachelines early which prolongs the lock duration and harms other threads attempting to acquire the same contended cacheline. Conversely, lazy execution (waiting until the atomic is oldest in the load queue and the store buffer is empty) minimizes cacheline lock time but exposes full memory access latency on non-contended accesses.
motivation: With fence-free atomic implementations now in modern x86 processors (confirmed experimentally), the new performance question is not whether to remove fences but when to issue the atomic: eager execution doubles performance on non-contended workloads like canneal/freqmine, while lazy execution nearly halves execution time on contended workloads like pc/sps; a static policy always leaves half the benefit on the table.
method: Rush or Wait (RoW) uses a small hardware table (64 entries, each with a 4-bit counter, indexed by hashing the instruction's program counter) to predict whether to execute atomic instructions immediately (eagerly) or wait (lazily) based on how much contention—other threads competing for the same data—is expected. It learns contention patterns by detecting three signals: when other cores interrupt the data while locked, when they request data during instruction preparation (monitored via the Atomic Queue), or when data arrives slowly from another core's cache exceeding 400 cycles. Store-to-load forwarding from older instructions can override lazy predictions to improve locality. The mechanism needs only 64 bytes of total storage.
key_novelty: This work proposes the first hardware predictor that dynamically chooses between eager (immediate) and lazy (delayed) execution of atomic operations by predicting cacheline contention, using only 64 bytes of state.
contributions: Experimental characterization on real x86 hardware showing that modern processors implement fence-free (unfenced) atomic RMWs
Analysis of the eager-vs-lazy trade-off: eager wins for non-contended atomics (up to 2x speedup), lazy wins for contended atomics (up to 2x speedup), with strong workload dependence
Three-tier contention detection: execution window, ready window, and coherence-directory latency threshold for comprehensive contention tracking
RoW hardware mechanism achieving 9.2% average (up to 43%) execution time reduction over always-eager baseline with only 64 bytes of storage overhead

metrics.speedup: 9.2% average execution time reduction (up to 43%) vs eager atomic baseline across Splash-4, PARSEC 3.0, and fine-grain synchronization benchmarks
metrics.other: RW+Dir Sat achieves 7.3% reduction vs eager; 5.5% vs lazy; modeled on 32-core Intel Alder Lake parameters

baselines: Eager atomic execution (as soon as operands ready)
Lazy atomic execution (wait until oldest + SB empty)
limitations: Evaluated only on synchronization-intensive parallel benchmarks from Splash-4, PARSEC, and custom suites; impact on workloads with mixed atomic patterns (some contended, some not at the same PC) is limited by predictor aliasing with 64 entries.
primary_theme: contention-aware dynamic eager/lazy scheduling of atomic RMW instructions
